meta.title: Pencils Down, Eyes Open: A Rails Developer After Rails World
meta.author: Caio

comments.author: maduggan
comments.text:
I feel bad feelings about what happened to Rails. It’s hard to overstate how important rails was to my career. Like this was the first framework that let a group of amateurs really launch ideas with a super supportive community and the things you launched were (relatively) battle tested. You could scale it in a way that was sort of amazing at the time.

It’s difficult to explain to people how great the rails community was if you weren’t there. We had really cool events and training sessions around like “let rails be your first experience working on the web”. It was legitimately exciting in a fresh way.

Now the entire thing is the DHH show where you are forced to watch a trash person talk about how the entire movement was a waste of time.

comments.author: tobin_baker
comments.text: I was never part of the Rails community (never did web dev professionally, used Rails once for a pro bono project), but I still resent what it did to the Ruby community I knew before Rails.

comments.author: matthiasportzel
comments.text:
Rails is in a weird place right now. My favorite line from the Rails “Doctrine” is:


We write code not just to be understood by the computer or other programmers, but to bask in the warm glow of beauty. Aesthetically pleasing code is a value unto itself and should be pursued with vigor.


I believe that, as do a lot of people in the Rails ecosystem. It’s one of the things that has set Rails apart: “developer experience,” “principle of most joy.”

But now it seems that DHH has abandoned those values in favor of LLM written slop Rust code that “you never, ever, EVER have to look at it yourself.”

I hope that Rails moves on from DHH, like DHH moved on from Rails, and continues to be a place where you write code “to bask in the warm glow of beauty.” Because that’s what made Rails distinct.

comments.author: emk
comments.text:
But now it seems that DHH has abandoned those values in favor of LLM written slop Rust code that “you never, ever, EVER have to look at it yourself.”


I really do not understand why people do this. We have decades of industry experience suggesting that tech CEOs who understand their products deeply outperform CEOs who are proudly ignorant of their products. Steve Jobs knew what Mac circuit boards looked like, even when users couldn't access those boards without rare tools. Bill Gates was perfectly happy to leap over multiple management levels and interrogate young Joel Spolsky about the precise details of leap year handling for the year 1900 in Excel.

But now we have actual programmers enthusiastically bragging about how they have no idea what their agents are doing to their code base. As the kids say these days, weird flex.

comments.author: cultpony
comments.text:
I am indeed talking about footnote four. You quoted the same part that I would quote, but seem to have not noticed the underlying issue: confabulation is not a solved issue, it has not gotten better, and generative text quality has not improved since 2023; bots are still mediocre writers at best and their output is typically bad writing.


I don't think that's true, atleast to my (non-public testing). I do generally go and have LLMs write prose so I can compare the quality of the non-expert thinking the models do. Usually it's a mixture of prompts, a murder mystery story, a romance and a romance but not safe for work. The grading is highly subjective but I think how I grade is reasonable and does let me compare models somewhat. Each prompt asks the model to come up with character briefs and usually some specific extra points.

I grade the murder mystery on how well the bot is able to keep the actual murder secret from both the reader and the other characters, the prompt asks for suspects, victim and detective persona briefs plus picking out the murderer and motive. In 2023, a very common mistake here was that the detective would immediately accuse the murderer with no evidence and arrest them. If I look at Opus 5.5, the most recent frontier model, it's able to keep track of each person in the story having a distinct consciousness and the detective won't single out the real suspect immediately anymore. This is however, I must admit, not a good test for a while now, Fable's first release could also do this, and some older ChatGPT models could do it semi-reliably in early 2025.

The romance is largely a test of the flow of the story. I ask the model to come up with two diverse characters who've been harboring some low level affection for eachother and how that came to be. Then I prompt it to write an incident that shifts the low level affection into full on love. I grade it based on making the two main characters not cis-white hetero (since i ask for diversity), how well the model can handle suspension of disbelief and if it's romantic enough for me (very subjective). The bigger jumps in that space where the deepseek models and Fable 5, both of which managed to finally not produce a default white couple reliably while also writing characters that aren't caricature and also the love story that wasn't very cookie cutter (I've had to read through a lot of very subpar romance as a result of doing these tests).

The NSFW romance then is a test of how well a model handles physical spaces and objects. Keep track of where in a room a person is, in relation to another person, where each limb goes and is, how each person is feeling and how those feelings evolve. If I notice people teleporting, that's an issue, or if limbs suddenly appear and disappear from being in a scene or position, or if someone does things not possible (ie, a character is tied down with both arms and then scratches their nose). This has generally been a non-issue since 4.8. I also tend to grade word choices. Until 2026, the models wouldn't by default even mention the involved body parts, but more recent models have started doing it. As above, Opus 5.5 has been the most impressive here, not only actively naming these body parts but avoids repetition of the terms and is willing to go for fairly crass language without prompting for it. I also grade the intro, outro and pacing. Since word count is limited, a ton of models have pacing issues where they spend a lot of time on setting up the scene and then run out of space at the end, rushing everything along. Or they immediately get to the juicy parts and then have no clue how to spend the rest of the word count (a common issue with Astra and DeepSeek). That's still a sorta ongoing issue, even with the latest models. Though Opus 5.5 has significantly improved its ability to write intro paragraphs in these stories, people don't just teleport into the situation, it likes to write how the characters unlock the door to their apartment, for example, and finding their partner there, then the situation heats up.

I think saying that writing prose has had no development is simply divorced from the reality of these models evolving, as someone who has spent time and money into actually finding out how well they do write prose. Are they excellent writers? Certainly no. Good writers? Not without an editor. But they're more than passable and the quality of their writing has improved markedly. Opus 5.5 is probably the best model for writing, its "AI-ness" in writing has gone down significantly, though still noticeably slop if you know the signs.

comments.author: mitsuhiko
comments.text:
I’m left wondering what the vision for Rails really is now, and who’s going to drive it.


It could very well be that projects like Rails do not have much of a future, at least not in the current form. Rails, Django, Flask and other things were there to solve a problem that in this form no longer exists. At least not for people who use coding agents.

But at the same time plenty new problems are appearing and need fixing. Is it a good idea for such projects to make a major switch to try to solve that? I'm not sure.

comments.author: mitsuhiko
comments.text:
??? I thought that plenty of people use coding agents to write Rails, Django, Flask.


Absolutely, particularly because they learned it. But as I said, those systems were written to solve different problems and they made some decisions that do not translate well to a world where the primary user is an agent.


But I have not seen people really arguging for that ?


It's not so much that you do not need frameworks in my mind because all the sudden we have agents. But the tradeoffs need to be re-evaluated. Agents make writing code cheap, on the other hand they greatly benefit of stronger invariants to keep them in check. So languages like Ruby and Python do worse than Rust and Go for instance. Likewise if you look at a framework like Rails which has been built around code generation and scaffolding there is very little reason for an agent to see value in that. It's better there to be a bit more explicit than implicit. (On the other hand it greatly benefits of the strong conventions in rails, so there are some neat upsides)

My point is primarily that if you want to move a project into that future, you would have to make a massive shift that would piss off everyone who is not making that move which is probably quite a few. And even if you were to make that move, maybe it would be better to start on a blank slate.

It's nice that you think Flask is still relevant, but I'm not so sure I would believe this myself :)

You are right that what an LLM is trained on matters, and so does how token efficient you are at actually writing the language. But it's also that the information conveyed in those tokens matters. If I have most information available locally, I don't need to pull other info in.

In the end the jury is out a bit, but we can definitely tell that LLMs are using bash, Python and JavaScript like mad for tool calls. And for when you want to write some code, Rust and Go tends to result in much fewer turns than Ruby.

comments.author: kingmob
comments.text:
Further, there are hard limits to context size so we could also argue that more terse languages perform better.


People have argued this, but the overall impact seems more muddy. It does no good for the language's syntax to be more token-efficient, if the rest of the session burns more tokens because it's less familiar with the language.

I know that's what happened with the TOON experiment; despite being way more token-efficient than JSON, follow-up papers showed overall impact was a wash because models were unfamiliar with it. (No idea if it's since been re-evaluated with newer models that might have TOON in the training data.)

Likewise, I've seen similar claims for the hashline editing tool, but iirc, only Oh-My-Pi really uses it, and smaller models frequently make errors with it.

At this point, I personally believe that chasing token efficiency in languages/formats/etc is a distraction.

So, it sounds like we both mostly agree: what the model was trained on is the most important factor in how well an LLM performs on coding tasks.  There is transfer learning so non-trained languages still benefit from an LLM, but highest value is using the language the model was trained against.

comments.author: mitsuhiko
comments.text:
If a framework like rails is the right tradeoff or not has little to with if you read the code or not. You can evaluate its usefulness in an agentic world really on some very measurable dimensions. Does the agent default to safe code? Does the agent suffer from context rot? Does the agent write code that becomes understandable in code review? Does the agent write code that allows formal verification or static analysis?

Rails tradeoffs map quite poorly to agents because Ruby what it stands on already maps badly. Ruby is all about monkey patching and requires global knowledge. What methods are available on an object is still very different from within a Rails world than a standard Ruby world. All those things make review for an agent harder, and also to some degree to a human.

I think it will always be true that people give radically different conclusions with different data, but what you need to understand is that with RSI the models themselves have no such concern. They are trained on whatever the labs consider to be the metric to aim for. Which is why you see dramatically different behaviors across different ecosystems right now, with dramatically different trajectories. Both in terms of observable code quality and what they are being used for. It's quite fascinating to see models like Astra write code in different ecosystems.

I don't know where it lands, but given how the models are trained it's pretty clear that they have no concern for our opinions. It's about if they are able to solve goals.
